sections.h2: What does an Ohio quitclaim deed actually transfer?
sections.html:
It transfers whatever interest the signer has, no more. R.C. 5301.02 says a grant of land conveys the entire interest the grantor could lawfully convey unless the deed clearly shows a smaller estate was intended. A quitclaim does not add anything to that: if the grantor owns half, the grantee gets half.

The Revised Code prints statutory forms for three other deed types, and each one carries named promises. The general warranty form in R.C. 5302.05 brings covenants that the grantor holds the land in fee simple, that it is free of encumbrances and that the grantor will defend title against all claims. The limited warranty form in 5302.07 narrows those promises to claims arising through the grantor. The fiduciary form in 5302.09 is for executors, administrators, trustees, guardians and receivers.

Those covenants arrive only when the deed says so. R.C. 5302.06 gives the words "general warranty covenants" the full meaning of the promises listed there. A deed without such words leaves the buyer relying on the title the grantor really has.

sections.h2: How is an Ohio deed signed and acknowledged?
sections.html:
The grantor signs, and the signature is acknowledged before an authorized official. R.C. 5301.01 lists the officials: a judge or clerk of a court of record in the state, a county auditor, a county engineer, a notary public or a mayor. The official certifies the acknowledgment and signs the certificate.

The statutory forms show what a clean Ohio deed contains. Each names the grantor with marital status and county, recites consideration, names the grantee with a tax-mailing address, describes the land, cites the prior instrument by volume and page, and carries the dower release for a spouse where one applies. The statute does not print a separate quitclaim form in the sections reviewed, so the same elements are the safe checklist for any Ohio deed.

When the grantor has received written notice that the property violates a building or housing code, R.C. 5301.253 requires written notice of the violations to the grantee before the transfer agreement, or before the deed is filed if there is no written agreement. A notice on the issuing authority's public records also binds later owners without further notice.

sections.h2: Where does an Ohio deed get recorded, and what does recording cost?
sections.html:
The deed goes to the county recorder in the county where the land sits. R.C. 5301.25 adds that until recording, a deed is fraudulent against a later good faith purchaser who had no knowledge of it. Recording is what protects the new owner, so a signed but unrecorded quitclaim leaves a gap.

The recorder's fees come from R.C. 317.32. For the standard recording and indexing of an instrument the statute lists:

  • A base fee of seventeen dollars for the first two pages, plus a housing trust fund fee of seventeen dollars.
  • Four dollars base plus four dollars housing trust for each later page.
  • A document preservation surcharge of up to five dollars, which a county may charge.

The deed must also pass through the county auditor's office first. When a survey was made of the land, the auditor requires the surveyor's name to appear in the deed, in a statement such as "A survey of this property was made by" followed by the name.

sections.h2: Who pays the Ohio conveyance fee on a quitclaim?
sections.html:
The grantor pays. R.C. 319.202 says the grantor covers the fee under 319.54(G)(3) and any county real property transfer tax, and the amount is collected when the statement of value is filed with the auditor. The mandatory fee is one dollar or ten cents per hundred dollars of value, whichever is greater, per R.C. 319.54.

A county may add its own tax under R.C. 322.02, capped at thirty cents per hundred dollars, paid by the grantor to the auditor before the deed goes to the recorder. Ask the auditor in your county whether the extra tax is levied there.

"Value" has a defined meaning. For a sale it is the full consideration, including any mortgage on the land. For a gift in whole or part it is the estimated open market price. Falsifying the value is prohibited. The same statute adds fifty cents for each transfer or entry, paid by the person requiring it.

sections.h2: Which Ohio transfers are exempt from the conveyance fee?
sections.html:
Several are, and many are the transfers people make by quitclaim. The statute spells out each exemption, and when one applies only a statement of the reason is required on the form.

Selected conveyance fee exemptions in R.C. 319.54(G)(3)
TransferStatute letter
To confirm or correct a deed already recorded(c)
Gift between spouses, or parent and child or the spouse of either(d)
Pursuant to court order, when not a result of a sale under that order(f)
Where no money or other valuable consideration is paid and it is not a gift(m)
Among heirs or devisees of one decedent with no money paid(s)
To a trustee when the grantor reserved an unlimited power to revoke(t)
On sale for delinquent taxes or assessments(e)

The full list in section 319.54 is longer. It also covers transfers to or from government bodies, transfers that only secure or release a debt, and several corporate and trust transfers.

sections.h2: When do survivorship and transfer on death options beat a quitclaim?
sections.html:
For a family transfer meant to take effect at death, Ohio has statutory tools that a plain quitclaim does not match. R.C. 5302.20 creates survivorship tenancy when a deed or will shows clear intent that the survivor takes the whole. The word "or" between two grantees does not do it alone. A conveyance from fewer than all survivorship tenants to an outsider passes the grantor's interest only on condition that the grantor survives.

A transfer on death designation affidavit under R.C. 5302.22 lets an owner name beneficiaries who take title at death. It needs no consideration and no delivery, but it must be recorded with the county recorder before the owner dies, and the recorder charges the same fee as for a deed. The affidavit must be verified before a person who can administer oaths.

A quitclaim made now gives the grantee a present interest, and the conveyance fee exemptions in the table apply to family gifts. Whichever route is used, a deed does not clear taxes: the lien for the year's tax attaches on January 1 and stays until paid, a point covered in the lien statute.

faqs.q: Can I use a quitclaim deed to sell my Ohio house?
faqs.a: Yes, any signed, acknowledged and recorded deed can carry a sale, but a quitclaim gives the buyer only the title you hold, with none of the covenants a warranty form carries. Ask your title company which form the buyer's lender will accept.

faqs.q: Does an Ohio quitclaim deed need to be notarized?
faqs.a: It needs an acknowledgment before a judge or clerk of a court of record, a county auditor, a county engineer, a notary public or a mayor. A notary is the common choice. The signing must be acknowledged for the deed to be recorded.

faqs.q: Does a quitclaim deed remove a mortgage or tax lien in Ohio?
faqs.a: No. The county's lien for each year's tax attaches on January 1 and continues until paid, whoever holds title. Check the payoff with the treasurer and your lender before transferring.

faqs.q: Is there a conveyance fee on a deed between family members?
faqs.a: A gift between spouses, or between a parent and child or the spouse of either, is exempt. A transfer with no money or other valuable consideration that is not a gift is also exempt. A statement of the reason goes on the form.

faqs.q: Where do I record an Ohio quitclaim deed?
faqs.a: Record it with the county recorder where the property lies, after the auditor endorses it. Until recorded, it is treated as fraudulent against a later purchaser without knowledge of it. Ask the recorder for current page counts and fees.
